newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin should avoid fat but can have odd drink.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin should avoid fat but can have odd drink.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin will have to steer clear of fatty foods but should survive an occasional drinking binge, top U.S. cardiologist Michael DeBakey said on Thursday, predicting: "You're going to see a vigorous leader."

The strong-willed president is walking around his hospital room, insisting that doctors transfer him to more luxurious quarters. But medics have been able to rein him in so far, the Texan heart surgeon said after talking with Yeltsin.
"He was pushing, yeah, but he finally agreed," not to check out of his emergency room for another day, DeBakey said.
Yeltsin, 65, has dropped his cholesterol level under 200 with a month-long low fat diet and will be asked to cut down on his sausage intake for the rest of his life, DeBakey said.
But with his heart pumping normally after a quintuple bypass operation on Tuesday, Yeltsin should be able to eat borshch and take an occasional drink within a few days, DeBakey said.

Yeltsin should even be able to overindulge from time to time, said the 88-year-old surgeon, though he added that Yeltsin's liver and kidneys did not look like those of a heavy drinker, as the president has been widely reputed to be.
"Hopefully he'll moderate any excesses he may have had," DeBakey said.
"(But) I wouldn't expect an occasional experience of that kind to have an effect on his heart. You've got to have repeated excesses of that kind to have a risk effect."
Yeltsin has missed a number of meetings during his presidency, including one with half the Irish government, when foreign news media speculated that he was ill or drunk. The Kremlin always denied it.

But Yeltsin, who rocketed around the country during a presidential election campaign earlier this year, pumping into the air on a swing near the Arctic Circle and doing the twist with southern Russians, will soon be back to form.
"That doesn't mean I would advise him to go mountain climbing," DeBakey said. But Yeltsin will seem a "new man".
"You're going to see a vigorous leader."

Yeltsin signed a decree from his hospital bed on Thursday, the anniversary of the 1917 Bolshevik revolution, changing the name of the holiday from "Revolution Day" to "Day of Accord and Reconciliation".
DeBakey predicted Yeltsin could be back in the Kremlin in two to three weeks, though he said it takes six to eight weeks for most bypass patients to regain their energy and work normally.
On Wednesday DeBakey, who advised Russian surgeons on the operation, told CNN that Yeltsin could be playing his beloved tennis again within four months.

But the surgeon, who performed the first successful bypass in 1964, said he had seen enough patients to think that today's cooperative president eager to follow doctors' orders soon might be tempted to let unhealthy habits creep back into his life.
"I've been very disappointed (with patients)," he said.
"They start off doing pretty well, and they feel better and become more and more normal and the next thing you know they are acting like ordinary people again."
